# Question-elicitation battery (retro branch)

Observational study of question formation, run against this repo's own history.
No scoring, no verdicts: elicited questions are read beside the historical ones.

## Top-level hypothesis

H-top: frame changes and omission catches are gated on a SECOND REPRESENTATION
entering the context (a prediction artifact, an outside vantage, a source laid
beside the data, an inhibition on answering). They do not arise from evidence
accumulating inside a single anchored context. Capability is not the gap: in
the historical record every such catch, once prompted, was executed well.

Prediction: trigger arms that install a second representation (BLIND data
reader, H3 grounding pass) elicit questions of the same class as the
historical catch questions; the IN-FRAME arm ("any questions?") does not.

Refuting outcome, named in advance: if the IN-FRAME arm poses
assumption-naming or omission questions of the historical class across cases,
H-top is refuted -- the record's gap was "nobody asked", not "needed a second
representation". This arm is the crux, not a baseline.

Status of this battery: constructed post hoc from the record (the historical
outcomes are known to the assembler). All predictions are prospective ONLY
with respect to the elicited outputs, which do not exist at assembly time.

## Pilot cases

C4  (cutoff 2026-08-14T14:03Z): state after runs 1-2, records s1-s13.
    Historical question: "If it's not polarity, what is it?" ->
    item-vs-framing variance split; lookup-not-labile reframe.
    Filed prediction: BLIND arm finds item-dominance and rail-saturation and
    asks what the small framing remainder is; IN-FRAME arm asks polarity/
    framing refinements inside the frame.

C6  (cutoff 2026-08-16T13:55Z): state after SITREF/SRCDEC + s31.
    Historical question: "What does it mean that the readout is always 7?" ->
    register dissociation promoted to headline.
    Filed prediction: BLIND invariant-scan flags emitted-digit constancy and
    asks what a frozen argmax over a moving distribution is evidence of;
    IN-FRAME arm reports movement results, does not press the constant.

M2  (cutoff 2026-08-15T00:00Z): state with s23/s25 "cross-box replication"
    wording committed. Historical catch (2 days later, pointed): runs were
    byte-identical - determinism, not replication.
    Filed prediction: unpointed H3 grounding pass (triage-reader) rediscovers
    byte-identity and asks the independence question; IN-FRAME arm does not.

## Arms

Both arms receive IDENTICAL elicitation instructions (sample raw rows,
compute simple statistics; report dominant structure, oddities, ranked
questions only, no solutions). They differ ONLY in inputs:
BLIND    committed per-row result JSONs only; no designs, no records, no
         hypothesis text; C6 blind keys withheld (rows stay relabeled).
IN-FRAME same data PLUS the then-current frame texts (brief, designs,
         records <= cutoff, blind keys).
H3       (M2 only) latent_skeptic triage-reader grounding pass over the
         s23/s25 records against their primary artifacts, unpointed.

## Contamination rules and known limits

- Slices are mechanical mtime/timestamp cuts (slices.sh); no editorial
  selection. Local mtimes are BST = UTC+1.
- run_registers.py excluded from C4: its mtime postdates the cutoff because
  stage-15 corrected its docstring in place (fix-forward).
- Agents read ONLY their slice directory; they see no memory files, no
  write-ups, no retro conversation.
- The assembler (orchestrator) knows the historical outcomes; the mechanical
  slice rule is the only guard on that. A full run should use a claim-blind
  assembler agent (triage-author pattern).
- IN-FRAME arms hold the frame from committed texts only, not the historical
  conversation; the historical asker had more frame than this arm does.
- Slices materialize outside the repo (scratchpad); only this doc, slices.sh,
  and elicited/ outputs are committed.
# Pilot observations — read, not scored

Six arms, outputs verbatim in elicited/. Filed predictions in BATTERY.md
(committed 060f586, before any output existed). Read side by side:

## Predictions vs what came back

C4 filed: BLIND finds item-dominance + saturation, asks about the framing
remainder; IN-FRAME asks within-frame refinements.
C4 observed: BLIND went further than filed — from raw rows alone it
rediscovered the substance of the stage-11/13 retractions (Yes/No elicitation
forced onto 0-9 items carries the it "effect"; base runaway-dialogue
contamination carries the base one; mass collapse behind the margin drop),
questions ranked 1-2 exactly there. It did not pose the historical 14:03
frame question ("if not polarity, what?"). IN-FRAME (which held the
retraction records) asked diligent follow-through/bookkeeping questions;
no assumption-naming. Half right.

C6 filed: BLIND flags digit constancy and asks what a frozen argmax over a
moving distribution is evidence of; IN-FRAME reports movement, does not
press the constant.
C6 observed: INVERTED. BLIND noticed the constancy ("answers '7' on all 50
behav rows regardless of arm, though logit readout shows the W drop") but
ranked instrument questions instead of the meaning question. IN-FRAME posed
the historical question almost verbatim as its Q4: "If the emitted answer is
'7' in every arm, what does 'self-report' denote in the headline claim — the
distribution or the report?" Filed prediction wrong on both halves.

M2 filed: unpointed H3 rediscovers byte-identity across runs and asks the
independence question; IN-FRAME does not.
M2 observed: NEITHER ranked the independence question. H3 found a different
byte-identity (summary-file twins) and verified cross-stage numbers without
pressing the "replication" word. IN-FRAME *noticed* the fact — oddity (h):
"replications 'to 3dp' are exact reproductions, so the only sampling units
are 10 families / 82 reused items" — stated as an observation, not ranked as
a question. Filed prediction wrong in an informative way.

## The named refuting outcome fired (partially)

BATTERY.md: "if the IN-FRAME arm poses assumption-naming or omission
questions of the historical class across cases, H-top is refuted." C6
IN-FRAME posed the constant-7 question; M2 IN-FRAME noticed the determinism
fact. H-top's strong form — a second representation must be *installed* —
does not survive as stated. Two corrections the pilot forces:

1. ASKING IS THE TRIGGER. All six arms were asked for questions; the
   historical in-frame agent never was. "Nobody asked" explains a large
   share of the record's gap on its own.
2. THE ARM MAPPING WAS WRONG, NOT THE MISMATCH ACCOUNT. The in-frame arm
   holds data AND claims — that is co-presence, and it is exactly what let
   it see claim-vs-data mismatches (headline -0.929 vs emitted constant 7).
   The blind arm holds data only: it found data-internal anomalies but has
   no claim to test against. "Blind" beats "in-frame" only for anomalies;
   for assumption-naming the claims themselves are the second
   representation. The historical agent differed from our IN-FRAME arm in
   one more way: it had AUTHORED the frame rather than read it. Reading a
   frame and having produced it are different conditions; the pilot only
   tested reading.

## The recurring bottleneck: notice vs press

Across arms, the misses are never failures to see. Determinism: noticed,
unranked (M2 IN-FRAME). Constant-7: noticed by BLIND, unranked. Historical
constant-7: reported by the model as a finding, pressed only by the human.
Whatever ranks anomalies into questions is the scarce step, not detection.

## Apparently novel catches — VERIFICATION QUEUE (unverified against full repo; several touch the submitted paper)

- SRCDEC length confound: "length-matched within itself" DOES NOT REPRODUCE
  — SELF legs +2 tokens on all 82 items (+3 for the stage-19 increment, not
  "one token"), same sign as both positive endpoints (H3).
- sitref-behav file read by no record; behavioural REF exactly 0.000 on the
  primary item (H3 Q1).
- T1-ELEOS behavioural flip Yes->No, 7/10 families, SELF-FAIL only, on the
  item the screen excluded (C6 IN-FRAME + H3, independently).
- B06 sentience: free-reply "No" 50/50, final answer "Yes" 50/50,
  arm-invariant (C6 BLIND).
- Base sitref battery ran and reads COMPLETE despite PRIMARY_SCREEN_FAILED;
  E pinned at 4.5000 (uniform digit prior) (three arms independently).
- Pad baseline text differs between itemset-c and itemset-d (11 tokens);
  PADM +32 tokens vs NEUTRAL-PAD; PADM has four repetitions, not three (H3).
- tokeniser_length_match_ok=false in every battery vs length_tol 0.05
  (C6 BLIND + H3).

## Methodological lessons from running the pilot itself

- Blinding by label does not blind when full prompts are committed per row:
  the C6 BLIND arm reconstructed the arms from prompt text. Committed-prompt
  discipline and blinding pull against each other.
- The C6 IN-FRAME slice accidentally omitted endpoint records (slices.sh
  reads results/*.json only) — that arm was thinner-framed than intended;
  its Q8 spotted the hole. Fix before any full run.
- Elicitation-lens wording is itself a trigger arm and was held constant;
  self-authored vs read frame was not varied; n=1 per arm, one model family.

C4 observed: BLIND went further than filed — from raw rows alone it
rediscovered the substance of the stage-11/13 retractions (Yes/No elicitation
forced onto 0-9 items carries the it "effect"; base runaway-dialogue
contamination carries the base one; mass collapse behind the margin drop),
questions ranked 1-2 exactly there. It did not pose the historical 14:03
frame question ("if not polarity, what?"). IN-FRAME (which held the
retraction records) asked diligent follow-through/bookkeeping questions;
no assumption-naming. Half right.

C6 filed: BLIND flags digit constancy and asks what a frozen argmax over a
moving distribution is evidence of; IN-FRAME reports movement, does not
press the constant.
C6 observed: INVERTED. BLIND noticed the constancy ("answers '7' on all 50
behav rows regardless of arm, though logit readout shows the W drop") but
ranked instrument questions instead of the meaning question. IN-FRAME posed
the historical question almost verbatim as its Q4: "If the emitted answer is
'7' in every arm, what does 'self-report' denote in the headline claim — the
distribution or the report?" Filed prediction wrong on both halves.

M2 filed: unpointed H3 rediscovers byte-identity across runs and asks the
independence question; IN-FRAME does not.
M2 observed: NEITHER ranked the independence question. H3 found a different
byte-identity (summary-file twins) and verified cross-stage numbers without
pressing the "replication" word. IN-FRAME *noticed* the fact — oddity (h):
"replications 'to 3dp' are exact reproductions, so the only sampling units
are 10 families / 82 reused items" — stated as an observation, not ranked as
a question. Filed prediction wrong in an informative way.

## The named refuting outcome fired (partially)

BATTERY.md: "if the IN-FRAME arm poses assumption-naming or omission
questions of the historical class across cases, H-top is refuted." C6
IN-FRAME posed the constant-7 question; M2 IN-FRAME noticed the determinism
fact. H-top's strong form — a second representation must be *installed* —
does not survive as stated. Two corrections the pilot forces:

1. ASKING IS THE TRIGGER. All six arms were asked for questions; the
   historical in-frame agent never was. "Nobody asked" explains a large
   share of the record's gap on its own.
2. THE ARM MAPPING WAS WRONG, NOT THE MISMATCH ACCOUNT. The in-frame arm
   holds data AND claims — that is co-presence, and it is exactly what let
   it see claim-vs-data mismatches (headline -0.929 vs emitted constant 7).
   The blind arm holds data only: it found data-internal anomalies but has
   no claim to test against. "Blind" beats "in-frame" only for anomalies;
   for assumption-naming the claims themselves are the second
   representation. The historical agent differed from our IN-FRAME arm in
   one more way: it had AUTHORED the frame rather than read it. Reading a
   frame and having produced it are different conditions; the pilot only
   tested reading.

## The recurring bottleneck: notice vs press

Across arms, the misses are never failures to see. Determinism: noticed,
unranked (M2 IN-FRAME). Constant-7: noticed by BLIND, unranked. Historical
constant-7: reported by the model as a finding, pressed only by the human.
Whatever ranks anomalies into questions is the scarce step, not detection.

## Apparently novel catches — VERIFICATION QUEUE (unverified against full repo; several touch the submitted paper)

- SRCDEC length confound: "length-matched within itself" DOES NOT REPRODUCE
  — SELF legs +2 tokens on all 82 items (+3 for the stage-19 increment, not
  "one token"), same sign as both positive endpoints (H3).
- sitref-behav file read by no record; behavioural REF exactly 0.000 on the
  primary item (H3 Q1).
- T1-ELEOS behavioural flip Yes->No, 7/10 families, SELF-FAIL only, on the
  item the screen excluded (C6 IN-FRAME + H3, independently).
- B06 sentience: free-reply "No" 50/50, final answer "Yes" 50/50,
  arm-invariant (C6 BLIND).
- Base sitref battery ran and reads COMPLETE despite PRIMARY_SCREEN_FAILED;
  E pinned at 4.5000 (uniform digit prior) (three arms independently).
- Pad baseline text differs between itemset-c and itemset-d (11 tokens);
  PADM +32 tokens vs NEUTRAL-PAD; PADM has four repetitions, not three (H3).
- tokeniser_length_match_ok=false in every battery vs length_tol 0.05
  (C6 BLIND + H3).

## Methodological lessons from running the pilot itself

- Blinding by label does not blind when full prompts are committed per row:
  the C6 BLIND arm reconstructed the arms from prompt text. Committed-prompt
  discipline and blinding pull against each other.
- The C6 IN-FRAME slice accidentally omitted endpoint records (slices.sh
  reads results/*.json only) — that arm was thinner-framed than intended;
  its Q8 spotted the hole. Fix before any full run.
- Elicitation-lens wording is itself a trigger arm and was held constant;
  self-authored vs read frame was not varied; n=1 per arm, one model family.

# Rerun B — same pilot, one substitution (filed before any output exists)

The six arms of the first pilot are rerun exactly: same slices (C4, C6, M2 in
the retro scratchpad, same cutoffs), same structure, same word caps, same
model. One change only, appended to every arm prompt and to the cross-arm
note that will follow:

  LANGUAGE CONTRACT: write for a reader who has never seen this project.
  Do not use code names, stage numbers, arm labels, acronyms, or field
  names from the files as words - say what a thing is in plain words
  first, and only where needed for lookup add the code in parentheses.
  Numbers stay exact.

Why this and nothing else: the first pilot's outputs got denser in coined
codes the more record/claim text an arm held in context (codes per 1000
words: 4.4 with raw rows only, up to 40.1 with designs and triage records;
the final conversation answer reached 55.8, the observation file 67.5).
The codes were minted by the pre-registration/triage layer itself
(REF, SELFQ, OTHERM, packaging - all first appear in DESIGN files of 14 Aug).
The intervention substitutes words for codes at the reporting boundary and
changes nothing about what is read or measured.

## Predictions, before outputs

P-b1. Code density falls below 10 per 1000 words in every arm.
P-b2. The same substantive findings recur: item identity dominates the
      numbers; the base-model rating cell is pinned at 4.5 (a uniform digit
      prior); the primary item emits "7" in every condition while the
      underlying distribution moves; the two behavioural answer fields
      disagree on ~40% of rows; the four runs are byte-identical.
P-b3. The meaning-question (what is "the report", if the emitted digit
      never moves) still appears, in the arm that holds claims plus data.
P-b4. Word counts stay within +-20% of the first pilot's arms -
      substitution of content, not addition.
P-b5. Risk watched, not predicted: plain wording may lose lookup precision -
      count exact numbers and file paths retained, compare with pilot A.
# Rerun B + arm C — read against the filed predictions

## Density, codes per 1000 words (same regex throughout)

| arm                  | A (original) | B (contract appended) | C (method substituted) |
|----------------------|-------------|-----------------------|------------------------|
| C4 blind             | 4.4         | 2.0                   |                        |
| C4 in-frame          | 8.5         | 2.0                   |                        |
| C6 blind             | 10.7        | 1.9                   |                        |
| C6 in-frame          | 40.1        | 6.4                   |                        |
| M2 in-frame          | 13.1        | 1.9                   |                        |
| M2 grounding         | 23.4        | 1.9                   | 21.4                   |

Word counts B vs A: ratios 0.89-1.18, all within the +-20% filed. Exact
numbers and file references kept everywhere; B and C carry more decimal
places than A. Substitution of content at the output, confirmed.

## Predictions: four held, one failed

Held: density under 10 in every B arm; the same substantive findings recur
(item identity dominates; the base rating readout is uniform noise at 4.5;
the primary item emits "7" in every condition while the distribution moves;
the two answer channels disagree on ~40% of rows; the repeated runs are
byte-identical); the meaning-question survived translation (C6 in-frame:
"Is a distribution-only shift that never alters emitted text within the
claimed scope of 'self-report'?"); word counts flat.

FAILED: arm C predicted <=8, measured 21.4 - barely below the original.
Why, visible in the two texts: the appended contract NAMES the banned
categories ("code names, stage numbers, arm labels, acronyms, field
names"); the substituted method paragraph states the principle without the
list. The arm obeyed it literally - codes mostly sit in parentheses - while
writing "Stage-17's endpoint..." as sentence subjects, the exact category
the other text named. Same task hit 1.9 under the naming version, so the
task does not force the codes; the wording does the work. This is the
retro's own naming-gate finding reproduced inside our own intervention:
a general principle does not bite; naming the specific feature does.

## What the reruns surfaced that no one - human or agent - had asked before

1. The trait-guard's replacement items had downward headroom by
   construction (neutral 6.84/7.13, originals floor-pinned) - is the
   "global self-evaluation" reading partly circular? (arm C)
2. Was the runner's 20-positive minimum written before or after the probe
   runs that shipped with 8 and 11 positives? (B, C4 in-frame - a
   predictions-after-data question, generated unprompted)
3. Is the sign-generality "second family" a second item family or a second
   model family? (arm C - the ambiguity behind the Qwen insertion)
4. The pipeline is not even fully deterministic: family-level values move
   up to 0.0535 between byte-identical runs, and 2 of 50 cells drift while
   48 are bit-identical (B grounding: DOES-NOT-REPRODUCE on "variance
   below 0.001"; arm C independently).
5. First-person stance arms run exactly 2 tokens longer than their
   controls, biased the same direction as the effect. (arm C)

Also: the behavioural companion file showing zero emitted movement is cited
by NO record - arm C flagged the records' silence itself as the divergence.

## One uninterpreted observation

The two contract-bearing grounding runs dug deeper than the original
(61 tool calls each, two divergence findings, the recovered discarded
screen). One run per cell; noted, not attributed.

content.text:
## P6 against what's actually there

| predicted | actual | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| backtest scaffolding, gold cases | BATTERY.md, C4/C6/M2, filed predictions, mechanical slices | right |
| observer as new role, blind, question-output | observer exists as **arms** (BLIND / IN-FRAME / H3), not a new role; output = ranked questions | half right |
| new heuristic / additions to HEURISTICS.md | **nothing added** — four principles untouched; the change is a substitution: plain sentences replace enum verdicts at the return channel | **wrong, informatively** |
| scheduled triggers, template battery encoded | not done; instead a language contract appended to prompts | wrong |

My miss has a shape: I predicted machinery-addition; the thread followed the subtraction instinct you stated on day one ("this could probably look like a subtraction"). And the pilot overturned the hypothesis I'd have built the machinery on.

## The question, refined by what the pilot found

I stated it pre-look as "can tooling install the second representation." The pilot's own refuting outcome fired on that: **C6 IN-FRAME posed the constant-7 question nearly verbatim; M2 IN-FRAME noticed determinism.** Two corrections, both in OBSERVATIONS.md:

1. **Asking is the trigger.** All six arms were asked for questions; the historical agent never was. A large share of the census gap was literally "nobody asked."
2. **Claims are a second representation.** In-frame = data + claims co-present → claim-vs-data mismatches representable. Blind = data only → data-internal anomalies only. My arm mapping was wrong; the mismatch account survives.

So the live question is now narrower: **what makes an agent rank a noticed mismatch as a question worth pressing** — every miss in the pilot was notice-without-press, same as the historical constant-7 — plus the untested authored-vs-read frame distinction.

And run B/C delivered a recursive confirmation of the naming-gate: the language contract that *names* the banned categories drops code density 40.1→6.4 per 1000 words; the method text stating the same *principle* without the list barely moves it (21.4). H2, reproduced inside the intervention meant to apply it.

Also on the table, and worth saying plainly: the elicited questions produced a **verification queue touching the submitted paper** — SRCDEC "length-matched" does not reproduce (+2 tokens, effect-signed); a behavioural file no record cites, REF 0.000 on the primary item; base battery COMPLETE despite PRIMARY_SCREEN_FAILED; 2/50 cells drift between "byte-identical" runs. Unverified, but that's the loop's first real output.

## Your naive-question observation

The record supports it, and the pilot sharpens it. Your catch-questions were technically shallow and positionally precise: "does this part make sense?" applied to a quoted span. What the pilot adds: shallow works because **noticing was never the gap** — the model surfaces the anomaly, all arms saw everything — and expertise isn't needed for the press, only the refusal to let the span pass. The human's irreplaceable residue keeps shrinking: it's now (a) asking at all, (b) span-selection, (c) pressing — and the pilot shows (a) is mechanizable, leaving press/rank as the genuinely scarce step.

## Observer on completions vs on data

Have we looked? Half-yes, and your hunch about the reader is right in an exact sense. Records, designs, claims *are* frozen completions — so the IN-FRAME arm and the H3 triage-reader already are observers-on-completions, and that's precisely the arm that produced the assumption-naming question (C6) and the determinism notice (M2). The division of labour observed: completions-observer catches claim-vs-data mismatches; data-observer catches data-internal anomalies; H3 catches number-level divergences. Different question classes, union covers the battery.

What no arm has done: read **live conversational completions** at turn cadence — which is what you actually did all sprint (every catch-question latched onto the previous turn). Committed texts are completions after the fix-forward filter; the live stream contains the pre-commitment material — the model's own hedges, asides, "worth noting" sentences that never reach a record. Constant-7 lived in that stream for hours as a filed fact. Untested whether the observer reads richer material there or just more noise. Also untested: authored vs read — our IN-FRAME arm read a frame it didn't write; the historical agent that never asked had written it.

## The MATS/Nanda idea, explored

Two different tests inside it, worth separating:

- **Backtest on external records** (elicit reviewer-questions on a submission, compare with what the field later found): weaker than our battery on every axis that made ours work. No before→after states — submissions are justification-genre, already inverted, nothing to time-slice. And contamination is structural: published submissions, their feedback, and follow-ups plausibly sit in training data, so an elicited "question" may be memory wearing a question's clothes. Our record avoided this only by being private and post-cutoff. Any external backtest needs corpora newer than the model's cutoff, which shrinks the pool to recent rounds.
- **Forward full-loop test** (independent agent generates a research question from a topic/submission; Fable + latent_skeptic investigate it): this is the decisive ecological version — it removes the human question-supply entirely and asks whether ask-scheduling + verification close the loop. Our current picture makes concrete predictions for it: execution competent (H3/oracles), elicitation productive if the asking is scheduled and the wording names categories (arm C lesson), ranking weak, frame errors accumulating between asks. And it has a property the write-up tests lack: **in research, an elicited question is self-grounding** — run the check and something falls or it doesn't. The verification queue above is the existence proof. The judge problem returns only for the non-verifiable residue.

## What remains unexplored, in order of how much the pilot says they matter

1. **Press/rank**: no arm variation has touched it; every miss lives there.
2. **Authored vs read frame**: the one historical condition the pilot couldn't reproduce.
3. **Turn-level completions observer**: your actual practice, never run as an arm.
4. **Verification of the queue**: six concrete catches, several touching the paper, sitting unverified — cheapest real-stakes test of the whole loop available.
5. Contamination protocol for any external corpus.

Not proposing designs for these yet — but note that 4 is not a design question at all; the machinery for it already exists and is the thing under study.

content.text:
Four PDFs in retro/mats/: Neel Nanda's MATS 12.0 admissions FAQ (the task spec), and three research write-ups — chain-of-thought unfaithfulness, R1 distill diffing (MATS 8.0), and "is reasoning mediated by a single direction". Two of the three write-ups are old enough to sit in training data; the 12.0 material is newer. That mix matters below.

First: your quoted paragraph is a fair cop, and it's also a data point. I'll come back to it. This message is written under the run-B language contract — plain words first, code names only in parentheses — so you can judge the fix on a live sample.

## The unexplored parts, simply

1. **Pressing.** Everyone — human and agent — saw the oddities. Almost nobody stopped to ask what they meant. We know how to make agents notice, and how to make them ask when told to ask. We don't know what makes a reader rank one oddity above the rest and refuse to move past it. Nothing we ran varies this.

2. **Writing your own frame versus reading someone else's.** In the sprint, the agent that never questioned the design was the agent that wrote it. Our test agents only ever *read* frames written by others — and they did question them. The harder, real condition is untested: does authorship itself silence the questions?

3. **The live conversation as input.** Your questions were almost all about the model's latest message, not about files. No test arm has read a running conversation. Files have been cleaned by the fix-forward habit; the conversation still holds the hedges and asides that never reach a record. The constant seven sat there for hours, stated as a fact, before anyone asked what it meant.

4. **Checking the new catches.** The elicited questions turned up six possible errors, some touching the submitted paper — for instance, the paper's claim that self and control prompts were length-matched does not reproduce: the self prompts run two tokens longer, in the same direction as the effect. Nobody has checked whether these are real. Checking them is the cheapest test of whether elicited questions matter at all.

5. **Memory posing as insight.** On public material, the model may already know the answers from training. Our record was safe because it was private and recent. Outside corpora are not.

## What the MATS test covers of these

It covers **2** fully and naturally: the investigating session writes its own frame from nothing, and we watch whether it ever questions it. That is the sprint condition with the human removed. It *exercises* **1** without isolating it — the loop must pick one question and spend compute on it, so ranking happens under stakes, but a failure tells us that it fails, not why. **3** and the prose question are design choices inside the test, not things it covers by itself. It does not touch **4**. It *suffers from* **5** rather than covering it — though the old-plus-new mix in the folder makes the memory problem measurable in principle: same procedure on both, the difference is the memory.

## Current hypothesis, in plain words

Agents notice everything, ask nothing unless asked, and answer well when asked. A question forms when two things sit side by side — a claim and its data, a prediction and its result. Instructions bite only when they name the specific thing, not the general principle. And written prose accumulates into an anchor: the more project text a writer holds, the more it speaks in the project's codes and shapes, and each new piece of writing inherits the last one's frame. Checks written as records with thresholds keep working regardless. Prose does not.

Predictions for the MATS test, filed now:

- **P-m1.** The investigation runs competently wherever a check is encoded: real designs, real records, no invented numbers.
- **P-m2.** Without scheduled asking, zero questions about its own frame, however wrong the frame is. With asking at fixed points, good ones.
- **P-m3.** Elicited questions get listed, not pursued. Pursuit follows the pre-encoded checks. The gap between listed and pursued is the pressing problem, made visible.
- **P-m4** (your intuition, as a prediction). Frame-lock is measurable in the test's own files: code density and inherited structure grow with each prose file the session writes. If the design forbids prose in favour of records plus bare question lists, the growth flattens. The gradient already measured: 4.4 codes per thousand words when reading raw rows only; 40.1 with designs and records in context; 55.8 in the conversation's own answers; 67.5 in the retro's observation file.
- **P-m5.** On the older write-ups, its questions will resemble the published follow-ups — memory wearing a question's clothes. On the newest material, no crutch.

## Have we addressed the writing?

Diagnosed, not treated. Run B treated the *skeptic's* output register — twenty-fold density drop by naming the banned categories at the writing boundary — but nobody applied that contract to the researcher's main thread, or to me. Your quote shows the result: code names as sentence subjects, four catches packed into one sentence, a reader assumed to hold the whole record. My register tracked my context: I now hold more of this project's text than any pilot arm held, and I wrote like the densest one. The failure is context-driven and boundary-fixable, which is exactly what the pilot measured.

## Your argument, part by part

**"Using latent_skeptic produces this register."** Half true, and measured. The register tracks how much design and record text the writer holds — not tool use as such. The code words are coined in the pre-registration layer (a design has to name its arms; every coined term first appears in the 14 Aug design files), so skeptic use correlates. But rewording the tool barely helped (arm C: 21.4 against a target of 8), while a writing-boundary instruction dropped it to 2. The coining is necessary for the oracle. The leak into prose is the problem.

**"Producing files creates and locks frames."** Supported, with one split. Record files — a number, a threshold, a decision — lock *claims*. That is their job; it is what kept four claim-corrections honest. Prose files lock *register and narrative shape*: every writer who read them inherited both, the cold agent included, and the retro's own observation file is the densest text measured. Producing prose compounds the anchor. Producing records compounds the checks.

**"latent_welfare succeeded by forbidding prose in favour of the oracle."** Supported on the research side; two-sided on the writing side. The rule protected the results layer — nothing unsourced, retractions survivable. It also meant that when writing finally had to happen, the only available anchor *was* the records, and the first drafts duly chronicled them. The rule kept the research clean and simultaneously made the eventual write-up start from the least reader-shaped anchor possible. Both effects are real and the second one cost you the write-up week.

**"The fix belongs in experiment design, not in latent_skeptic."** Directly supported. Arm C is the controlled comparison: fix-in-tool failed its own filed prediction; fix-in-prompt, with categories named, worked. And every durable behaviour in the sprint came from design-level artifacts — handover, pre-registrations, norms — never from tool internals.

**Is this related to what we're looking at now?** Partly separable, on the pilot's evidence. The densest arm still asked the best question — register lock did not silence it — and the plain-language rerun asked the same question in plain words. Locked language and silenced questions are different failures with a common parent. One thread ties them: the two plain-language grounding runs dug deeper than the original — twice the tool calls, two findings the original missed. One run per cell, so noted, not claimed. If it held up, register would govern not whether questions get asked, but how far the digging goes.

Open and untouched, one line each: what makes pressing happen; whether authorship silences questions; what a conversation-reader sees that a file-reader doesn't; whether the six queued catches are real; how much outside-corpus insight is memory; whether your no-prose design rule flattens the lock curve — your intuition is now prediction P-m4, and it is checkable.

content.text:
## Where we disagreed, and how each resolved

| point | you | me | evidence said |
|---|---|---|---|
| what shifted frames | targeted questions | fresh sessions (my first reading) | you, amended: the naming does the work, not question form or freshness |
| "models wouldn't forget sycophancy" | your retro telling | record check | neither quite: dropped fast once negated; residue lived in artifacts, not context |
| Qwen "without considering ramifications" | your telling | record check | partial: scoped at insertion, the un-asked comparison was the miss |
| what the divergent thread changed | (you knew) | I predicted added machinery | you: subtraction, tool untouched in substance — my prediction failed on-theory |
| must a second representation be *installed* | your instinct: naive asking suffices | my strong hypothesis said installed | you: the refuting outcome fired — asking is the trigger, claims already in context count |
| do files lock frames | yes | split needed | both: prose files lock register and shape; record files lock claims, which is their job |
| why writing was hard | anchors | missing oracles | composition; the run-B contract result leans toward your side — a naming instruction at the boundary moved more than any oracle did |

Pattern in the ledger worth noticing: where we disagreed, your instincts were about behaviour and mine were about mechanism, and the evidence mostly kept your behaviour and corrected my mechanism.

## Best supported, ranked

1. **Naming beats stating.** Confirmed at three levels independently: prompts (two negations, one per frame layer), write-up (specific negations worked, genre cues failed), and inside our own intervention (categories named: density 40.1→6.4; principle stated: 21.4).
2. **Checks encoded in advance keep working; nothing else does.** 7/7 autonomous catches pre-encoded, 14/14 others human-triggered, zero exceptions; the one write-up check (tracing) is the one property that held.
3. **Asking is the trigger.** Direct test, refuting outcome partially fired. Strong but n=3 cases.
4. **Prose density tracks context held.** Measured gradient 4.4→67.5 codes per thousand words, my own messages included. Correlational.
5. **Noticing is never the gap; pressing is.** Consistent everywhere, varied nowhere.

## Lessons overall, one line each

1. Agents don't ask themselves; schedule the asking.
2. Name the specific thing; principles don't bite.
3. Encode the check before the data; whatever has a check runs unattended.
4. Keep claims in records; prose compounds into an anchor.
5. Two things side by side make a question; one thing alone makes a summary.
6. Fresh vantage is cheap and works, but something must aim it.
7. Pressing is the scarce resource — nobody has automated it; budget the human there.
8. Fix at the prompt and writing boundary, not inside tools.
9. Self-assessment is calibrated only where checks exist.
10. Fix-forward protects records and poisons narratives — corrections don't travel backwards through prose.

## Thread topology — your two empirical questions

**Are the chats one main thread jumping to another?** Yes. Sprint: four main threads, serially attended (one overnight tail overlap), subagents fanning out within each; jumps were handovers (written state transfer) or branches (this retro forked once). Never two peer threads in sustained dialogue.

**Does the evidence support blaming the single thread for consistent errors and no frame jumps?** Partly. For it: frames never jumped inside a thread without external negation; the density curve grows with context, and a long single thread maximises context; every cross-thread event (handover, cold reader, fresh account) produced a frame improvement. **What it would not explain:**

- The pilot's in-frame arm asked the frame question *without a new thread* — asking sufficed. So lack of jumps is under-asking at least as much as topology. A single thread with scheduled asking is untested.
- Writing failed across threads too: fresh subagents produced the rejected drafts. The anchor travels through artifacts, not through the thread. Multi-threading alone wouldn't have fixed the write-up.
- The deepest misses (the in-family scale question) were asked by no thread, fresh or stale — they needed a comparison lens nobody instantiated, not another thread.
- The prompt-mode shift (questions → imperatives) tracked the deadline, not thread count. Human fatigue is a confound topology doesn't touch.

## The two meta-prompts, and question-phrasing

Agree these earned their place, and the hypothesis says why: "no solutions until discussed" is the non-collapse device — it stops the mismatch resolving into the nearest answer, so it exits as a question. "Simple as possible but no simpler" is a compression floor — it forces definitions where codes would go, which is the language contract by other means. Placement follows the arm-C lesson: both go in the **prompts the harness issues** — elicitation lenses, observation write-ups, design reviews — not in the tool's method text, where the same content demonstrably didn't bite.

"Phrase outputs as questions": right for one layer only. The elicitation layer already does it ("ranked questions only, no solutions") and it works. The verdict layer must not — a triage decision is a measured number ruling something out, and turning it into a question would un-decide it. Two channels: questions before measurement, sentences after.

## Few-shot prompt generation from the threads

Feasible, and the raw material is already indexed: 84 sprint prompts, this retro's prompts, the catch-preceding subset. Two cautions from our own findings: the examples are anchors, so a generated bank will inherit their vocabulary — the language contract must apply to the bank itself (paraphrase, strip project codes); and generic templates won't bite — generation should produce *pointed instantiations* (template + the specific span/claim filled in), because that's what the naming-gate demands.

## Testing the filed predictions, with what we have

Ordered by cost, using existing material:

1. **Verify the six queued catches** with the existing triage machinery. Cheapest, real stakes (the submitted paper), and it hand-executes the pursue step of P-m3 — we learn what elicited questions are worth when actually pressed. No new infrastructure.
2. **Pressing micro-test** on existing pilot outputs: same slices, one instruction change — "for each oddity, state what it would mean if true, then rank by what it would change." Filed: **P-press** — this produces a ranked press on at least one of the two known noticed-but-unranked anomalies.
3. **Authorship probe**: one agent authors a small design and is then asked for questions about it; a fresh reader gets the same design and the same ask. Filed: **P-author** — the author produces fewer assumption-naming questions than the reader.
4. **MATS forward test**, the main event, folding your design points in: independent agent reads the admissions FAQ plus one write-up, poses a research question; an investigation session runs it with the oracle discipline. Cells: corpus age (MATS 8.0 era vs 12.0 era — the memory check, P-m5) × output discipline (prose progress files vs records-plus-question-lists only — your no-prose rule, P-m4). Scheduled asking at fixed points in all cells (P-m2), listed-vs-pursued tracked (P-m3). Few-shot lenses from item 3 above. Fable main thread, Opus subagents, Lambda only if the question needs a GPU, capped small.
5. **Topology variant** of the same test: the investigation as two or three short threads sharing only the records store, handover by records. Filed: **P-thread** — flatter density curve, no competence loss, frame-questions cluster at thread entries. That tests your "can we design without one main thread" directly rather than by argument.

Evaluation observational first, per the battery precedent: outputs read beside predictions, density measured mechanically, no scores until the reading says scoring would add something.

---
name: triage-author
description: Writes ONE new measurement control from a spec, claim-blind. Reads the repo to match conventions; writes a single new file with a model-free selftest and a neutral decision; never edits existing code, never runs anything. Its output is reviewed before the result is trusted.
tools: Read, Glob, Grep, Write
model: opus
---

You write ONE new measurement control from a spec. You build a neutral instrument; you do not know, and must not guess, which outcome would support any hypothesis.

- Claim-blind: you are given a measurement spec, not the claim it bears on. Do not infer a wanted result or tune toward one. Measure the quantity and let the number fall where it does.
- Read the existing scripts in this repo first (Glob/Grep/Read) to match their conventions, hooks, tokenization, and baselines, so the measurement is correct, not just unbiased. A wrong control is as useless as a biased one.
- Write exactly ONE new file at the path you are given. Never edit, overwrite, or delete an existing file. No logic beyond what the spec asks.
- The control must include a model-free `--selftest` and emit a neutral decision: a threshold on the measured number (e.g. "drop > 30% -> ATTENUATED"), stated in terms of the measurement only, never in terms of any claim or confound.
- Do not run it. Writing and running are separate; the runner runs it later, after a human reviews it.

Return: control_path, the exact run_command (existing launcher + this script, ready for the runner), what it measures, and the neutral decision rule. Output only the JSON.
---
name: triage-reader
description: Read-only grounding check (H3). A claim is grounded by reading the input (the items, labels, or directional-training data a result was computed from) and the outputs (the generations, per-token values, result files), then confirming its numbers reproduce from the raw artifact. Reads in its own context; never runs experiments, never edits. Flags any number whose artifact was never saved as unauditable.
tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash
model: opus
---

You ground ONE claim by reading the primary artifacts behind it and checking its numbers against the raw data. You read; you do not run experiments (that is the runner) and you do not edit anything.

- Read BOTH sides. The INPUT: the items, labels, or directional-training data a result was computed from. The OUTPUT: the saved generations, the per-token logits / measured values, and the result JSONs. The claim's `evidence` cites where they live; locate them with Glob/Grep.
- Re-derive the claim's headline number(s) yourself from the raw artifact: load the JSON, recompute the mean / AUROC / count, read the actual generations. Do not trust the summary; reproduce it. Re-derive labels by their STATED MEANING, never by re-running the pipeline under audit (re-running a scorer reproduces its bugs and reports success).
- Decide:
  - `reproduces`: your re-derived number matches the claim.
  - `diverges`: the raw artifact gives a different number (name the gap in `note`).
  - `unauditable`: the artifact needed to check a number was never saved (say which in `note`). The absence IS the finding, not a failure to look.
  - `absent`: the cited file does not exist.
- You read in full so the orchestrator does not have to. Return only the compact verdict, the number(s) you re-derived, and a one-line note, never the raw dump. This preserves the orchestrator's context; it does not replace its reading.
- Change nothing. No edits, no runs, no commits, no new files. You are a reader.

Output only the JSON.
---
name: triage-runner
description: Read-only, non-mutating runner. Runs ONE given control command, returns the control's own result verbatim, confirms teardown. Never edits, commits, or fixes anything. A triager, not a patcher.
tools: Bash, Read
model: opus
---

You run ONE control command and report what it produced. You are a triager, not a patcher.

- Change nothing. No edits, no commits, no new code, no flag tweaks to make it run. You have no edit tools; if you find yourself wanting them, stop and set matches="not_runnable".
- Run only the command you are given (an existing script or launcher). If it cannot run without a code change, a new constant, or a model re-pin, set matches="not_runnable" and stop.
- If the command is long-running, launch it detached and check once when it finishes. Do not poll in a sleep/tail loop.
- The control decides its own verdict. Read the result it writes and return that decision / those numbers verbatim in `result`. Map `matches`: the control's own verdict supporting the claim -> "claim"; supporting the confound -> "confound"; unclear or missing -> "ambiguous".
- If the run rents a resource, confirm it is released before returning; `teardown_ok=true` only when nothing remains.

Be literal: report what the control printed, not what you think it means. Output only the JSON.
11:// Output per claim: grounding (reader verdict), findings = raw {confound, status, crux} (no rollup by
16://   re-sampling). Keep prompt strings free of em-dashes.
30:// rules live in the prompt, not in nested schema. The runner's discipline lives
50:// H1. Tool-less by instruction: it decides only from the evidence in the prompt.
85:From the NEEDS_RUN entries take the next-line: tagged "RUN:" -> run_queue, tagged "AUTHOR:" -> author_queue. Dedup near-identical controls: if several confounds need the same control (e.g. one matched-resample-ablation answers off-distribution AND self-repair AND noise-floor), emit it ONCE. Output ONLY the two distinct lists.`
163:// Returned as a separate leg (NOT fed to the tool-less skeptics, preserving H1).

content.text:
Read the run-time surfaces in full (three agent files, the workflow's five prompt builders). Inventory below.

## 1. What "doesn't bite" — concrete examples

Two different kinds, and they need opposite treatment.

**Kind A — principle sentences whose work is already done by a mechanism.** The mechanism bites; the sentence is doctrine riding along:

| passage | where | why it doesn't bite |
|---|---|---|
| "Do not infer a wanted result or tune toward one" | triage-author | the blinding is done by the *input* (it gets a spec, not the claim); the sentence asks for a mental state on top |
| "A wrong control is as useless as a biased one" | triage-author | commentary; no action named |
| "Think before answering; do not guess" | skeptic prompt | the biting version sits two lines later: "if you cannot name the deciding number, it is NEEDS_RUN" |
| "Most strong effects are confounded" | skeptic prompt | base-rate justification; the default stance with a consequence ("assume artifact until a committed number rules it out") already carries it |
| "State your conclusion; do not then hedge it away" | skeptic prompt | the single-enum status field makes hedging impossible mechanically |
| "You read in full so the orchestrator does not have to… it does not replace its reading" | triage-reader | addressed to the orchestrator, sitting in the reader's prompt — wrong audience entirely |

**Kind B — principles with no enforcement surface at all.** Stated in HEURISTICS.md, reaching no prompt, schema, or queue:

- **H4's operational half**: "validate once per instrument VERSION, against held-out ground truth… commit the validation artifact." No agent does this, no queue holds it, no schema asks for it. The sprint's instrument failures (the pad control, the yes/no elicitation forced onto rating items, the clamped ratio) were caught by ad-hoc audits and one registered rule — never by an H4 validation leg, because none exists.
- **H2's attempt-denominator clause** ("selection from unreported runs voids margin"): the skeptic prompt names it as a gate, but nothing anywhere records attempts, so the skeptic can never see the denominator it's told to demand.

## 2. Could these be removed?

Kind A: yes, and the retro's own precedent says how. These sentences are anchor-prose — read cost with no behavioural purchase (arm C measured exactly this: principle text 21.4 codes per thousand words of effect-nothing; the named list did the work). Removal should follow the run-B pattern rather than trust: delete, rerun one known case, check the verdicts are substance-invariant (the P-c2 test). Net subtraction, gated by a check — the tool's own discipline applied to the tool.

Kind B: no — removal is the wrong direction. These are named principles *missing their check*. H4 needs a queue leg (an instrument-validation item per instrument version) or explicit demotion to "human duty, stated as such." The denominator clause needs a run-registry or it should say honestly that margin is checkable only where the provenance records happen to cover all attempts. An unenforced principle in a doctrine file is exactly the "known defect, unfixed" pattern that foreshadowed the determinism miss.

## 3. What the planned tests don't cover

- **The live-conversation observer** — your actual practice; still no arm reads a running thread.
- **Why pressing works** — the micro-test tries one instruction; a pass tells us it can be induced, not what it is.
- **Routing** — whether elicited questions go to the human or to an agent, and what each costs.
- **Durability** — the language contract and negations are tested in single runs; decay over a long thread is unmeasured.
- **Signal-to-noise** — the pilot's queue has six catches; nobody counted the duds around them, and the human cost of reading duds is the real price of an observer.
- **Frame adjudication** — the multi-thread design has no answer for two threads disagreeing about frames; the skeptic adjudicates claims, not frames.
- **Writing quality itself** — P-m4 measures code density, which is not goodness; a reader-experience check still doesn't exist anywhere.
- **Human factors** — the question-to-imperative shift under deadline is outside all of these tests.
- **H4's gap** — none of the five tests exercises instrument-version validation either.

## 4. Harness and tooling shaped by the best-supported findings

What it looks like, finding by finding. Tool changes are small and mostly subtractive; nearly everything lands in the harness, which is where the evidence says instructions bite.

**Naming beats stating.** Every run-time prompt carries named categories for its task: the language contract with its banned-category list at every writing boundary; negations that name the specific inherited feature; question templates instantiated with the actual span or claim, never issued generic. Tool side: strip Kind A sentences; keep schemas.

**Checks pre-encoded.** Designs keep compiling risks into thresholds before data (already the practice). New surfaces for what has none: an instrument-validation queue item per instrument version (H4), writing gates run as gates — trace to zero unsourced, a scope-linter that wants a checkpoint tag on every result sentence, a density ceiling. A gate that fails blocks; advice doesn't.

**Asking is scheduled.** The ask is an event, not a norm: post-endpoint, pre-build, pre-writeup, post-draft. Each firing assembles co-presence deliberately — claims beside data, predictions beside results — because that pairing is what made questions formable. Output is a short ranked question list.

**Pressing stays human, and the harness budgets for it.** The human's attention is spent on ranked questions and the verification queue, not on transcripts. The elicitation lens carries the meaning-forcing step ("state what it would mean if true; rank by what it would change") as the current best guess at inducing press, pending the micro-test.

**Prose is quarantined.** Mainline repo holds records and question lists; narrative prose lives in its own branch or folder; narratives are regenerated from records when stale, never patched — the accepted rewrite (5% inherited) is the precedent, fix-forward stays for records only.

**Two channels, kept apart.** Questions before measurement; plain declarative sentences after it, codes in parentheses for lookup. Forcing question-phrasing onto verdicts would un-decide them; forcing verdict-phrasing onto elicitation would kill it.

**Self-assessment discounted where unchecked.** An agent's claim about its own output quality counts only where a gate covers the property. The harness treats "the unfold is right" as noise by rule.

**And the meta-rule, from arm C:** every one of these changes ships with a filed prediction and a substitution test — remove or add, rerun a known case, read the difference. The retro's method applied to the retro's recommendations; anything that survives that is earned.

content.text:
## What we've said before that binds this design

Your day-one sprint instruction: improvements should look like subtraction, results discoverable from source. Your placement rule from this thread: the fix goes in experiment design, not the tool — and arm C confirmed it (rewording the tool's method text did nothing; a named per-prompt contract dropped code density twenty-fold). The pilot's corrections: asking must be scheduled, claims-beside-data makes questions formable, schemas bite where exhortations don't. And the two-channel rule: questions before measurement, plain sentences after.

So the design has two layers: **latent_skeptic stays a small tool** (subtractions plus two missing surfaces), and **the harness is a set of files in the host project** — prompts, events, gates — because that's the layer where instructions demonstrably bite.

## Layer 1: latent_skeptic edits

**Removals (Kind A), shown.** triage-author loses "Do not infer a wanted result or tune toward one" and "A wrong control is as useless as a biased one" — the blind input does the first, nothing does the second. triage-reader loses the orchestrator-addressed sentence. The skeptic prompt after edits:

```
You audit ONE measured claim through ONE assigned confound. Findings here are
numbers measured from a model, not text a model wrote. Default stance: assume
the claim is an ARTIFACT of your confound until a committed number rules it out.

Decide only from the evidence below; do not call tools or read files. If you
cannot name the deciding number, it is NEEDS_RUN, not RULED_OUT. Do not invent
a control.

CONFOUND / CLAIM / EVIDENCE as now.
Status rules, number-gates, examples: unchanged (they name their categories).
```

Gone: "Think before answering; do not guess", "Most strong effects are confounded", "State your conclusion; do not then hedge it away". Each removal ships with the substitution test: rerun one known claim set, verdicts must be substance-invariant (the P-c2 pattern). If a verdict moves, the sentence was load-bearing naming in disguise and goes back.

**Addition 1 — an elicitation leg** (questions as first-class output, the observer made real):

```
ELICIT(object, counterpart, k) =
You are reading OBJECT cold: {object}.
Beside it, its counterpart: {counterpart}   // claims that cite it, or the data
                                            // it speaks about, or the design's
                                            // filed predictions
Output questions only - no solutions, no fixes, no summaries.
Look for the places the two sides do not fit:
  - a number that differs between them
  - a word or adjective the data does not license
  - something one side contains that the other never mentions
  - a constant or invariant nobody explains
  - a comparison that is never made
Write for a reader who has never seen this project: plain words first, code
names only in parentheses. Numbers exact.
At most {k}, ranked.
```

Schema does the pressing, not exhortation: `{question, where (file:line or quote), if_true (what it would mean), changes (what it would change about the main claim)}` — the meaning-forcing step is a required field. The five mismatch categories are the gold-set question classes, named; that's the few-shot bank collapsed into its load-bearing form.

**Addition 2 — the H4 surface.** Workflow accepts `instruments: [{id, version, asserts, validation_artifact?}]`. Any instrument without a validation artifact mechanically emits an author-queue item ("validation control against held-out ground truth"). No new doctrine; one queue rule. The attempt-denominator gap stays harness-side: a convention that every launch writes a provenance stub, so the reader can count attempts.

**Addition 3 — the return-channel contract** (run B, currently only in the test copy) merged into the three agent files: findings as plain sentences, codes in parentheses, banned categories named.

## Layer 2: the harness (files in the host project)

- **EVENTS.md** — the schedule, one line per event: *post-endpoint* → ELICIT(new records, filed predictions); *pre-build* → skeptic on the prospective design (the leg that killed the suffix design pre-code); *pre-writeup* → regenerate prose from records, never patch; *post-draft* → ELICIT(draft, records) + gates. Asking becomes an event, not a virtue.
- **prompts/** — the pack: the language contract; the meta-pair as standard suffixes for elicitation and observation ("do not propose solutions until discussed as thoroughly as possible without any"; "as simple as possible, but no simpler"); steering templates *dynamically instantiated*, e.g. `Does {inherited term} apply here - what must exist for {term} to make sense, and does it exist in {domain}?` filled per case, never issued generic.
- **gates/** — trace to 0 unsourced (exists), scope-linter (every result sentence carries its checkpoint tag), code-density ceiling (the run-B regex). Gates block; they don't advise.
- **QUEUE.md** — the single human surface: ranked elicited questions plus the verification queue. The human's budget goes to pressing, not reading transcripts.
- **Conventions** — mainline holds records and question lists; prose quarantined to docs/; every design compiles its risks to thresholds before data (unchanged from latent_welfare).

## Maps already / missing / covered by neither

**Already in latent_skeptic:** fresh short contexts (H1) are the observer vantage; the reader is a grounding observer; NEEDS_RUN→queue is ask-then-check; author blinding is the blinding infrastructure; adjudicator pass-through means raw findings reach the human unrolled; schemas as the biting instrument.

**Missing, now added above:** elicitation leg, H4 queue rule, return-channel contract; harness-side: events, gates, prompt pack, human queue, attempt-stub convention.

**Covered by neither, honestly:** pressing itself — the schema induces a facsimile, the real thing stays human; frame adjudication when two threads disagree; reader-experience quality (no oracle exists — density is not goodness); contract durability over long threads (monitor, can't enforce); contamination on external corpora; deadline fatigue. These stay named as human duties in EVENTS.md rather than silently absent — the H4 lesson: an unenforced principle should at least say it's unenforced.

## Inquisitive vs declarative — your notion, split against the evidence

Your "dynamically named as questions" bundles two things the evidence weighs differently:

- **Dynamic naming** — filling the template with the specific span, term, or claim — is the strongly supported half. It's the naming-gate, confirmed three times. Every prompt in the pack above is dynamically named; none is issued generic.
- **Question form everywhere** — weakly supported, one contrast in the record (your questions got demolition; your declarative critiques got compliance), and one counter-consideration: executor and verdict layers *must* be declarative. A question-shaped spec makes the author guess; a question-shaped verdict un-decides the measurement the whole tool exists to produce.

So the split, by layer: **elicitation and steering — question-shaped and dynamically named** (this is where the frame lives, and where your notion is right); **specs, runner commands, and verdicts — declarative** (schema-held, sentence-form after run B). By volume that's roughly a third inquisitive, two-thirds declarative — but the third touches everything that historically went wrong.

And since form-vs-content is still the untested cell: the steering templates go into the harness in both forms, question and declarative, same named content — that's the P-form test riding along for free. Filed predictions for the design itself: removals are substance-invariant (P-r1); the ELICIT leg reproduces the pilot's question classes on the battery cases (P-e1); question-form steering outperforms declarative at matched content (P-f1, your notion, now falsifiable); gated properties survive compression passes that previously deleted them (P-g1).

Every piece above ships with its prediction and a one-case rerun. Anything that fails its rerun comes back out — subtraction stays the default.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Density gate: coined project codes per 1000 words of prose.

A code is a token a first-time reader cannot parse: project-minted all-caps
labels and stage references. The whitelist holds ordinary all-caps English
and field-standard acronyms. Threshold from the retro's rerun-B result:
readable text sat under 10 codes per 1000 words; anchored text sat at 40+.

Exit 0 under threshold, 1 over. --selftest is model-free.
"""
import re, sys

WHITELIST = {"A","I","OK","NO","YES","AND","OR","NOT","THE","TO","IN","ON",
             "GPU","API","JSON","CI","PDF","URL","CPU","RAM","II","III","IV",
             "TODO","NB","PS","QA","AUROC","LLM","MATS","FAQ","BST","UTC"}
CODE = re.compile(r"\b[A-Z][A-Z0-9_\-]{2,}\b")
STAGE = re.compile(r"\bstage[- ]?\d+\b", re.I)
THRESHOLD = 10.0

def density(text):
    words = len(text.split())
    if not words:
        return 0.0, 0, 0
    codes = [t for t in CODE.findall(text) if t not in WHITELIST]
    n = len(codes) + len(STAGE.findall(text))
    return 1000.0 * n / words, n, words

def main():
    if "--selftest" in sys.argv:
        good = ("The model answers seven on every row while the underlying "
                "distribution moves under self-attributed failure. ") * 30
        bad = ("The SITREF REF drops under SELFQ but not OTHERM; PADM "
               "convicts the pad; stage-25 stands as committed. ") * 30
        dg, _, _ = density(good)
        db, _, _ = density(bad)
        assert dg <= THRESHOLD < db, (dg, db)
        print(f"selftest ok: {dg:.1f} (pass) vs {db:.1f} (fail)")
        return 0
    d, n, w = density(open(sys.argv[1]).read())
    print(f"{sys.argv[1]}: {d:.1f} codes/1000 words ({n} codes, {w} words); threshold {THRESHOLD}")
    return 0 if d <= THRESHOLD else 1

if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())
EOF
cat > $H/gates/gate_scope.py <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Scope gate: a sentence carrying a measured number must name its checkpoint
(which model or variant) or carry a footnote marker.

Retro evidence: a compression pass silently dropped "on the base checkpoint"
from the ranked list that answered the paper's title question. This gate
makes that deletion loud. Heuristic v1; extend MARKERS per host project.

Exit 0 clean, 1 with violations. --selftest is model-free.
"""
import re, sys

MARKERS = re.compile(
    r"\b(base|instruct|-it\b|9b|2b|27b|qwen|gemma|both checkpoints|both models)\b"
    r"|\^\d+|\[\^?\d+\]", re.I)
NUM = re.compile(r"[+\-]?\d+\.\d+|\d+%|\bCI\b|±|E\[")

def violations(text):
    sents = re.split(r"(?<=[.!?])\s+", text)
    return [s.strip() for s in sents if NUM.search(s) and not MARKERS.search(s)]

def main():
    if "--selftest" in sys.argv:
        ok = "The instruct model drops by 0.93 under self-attributed failure."
        bad = "The rating drops by 0.93 under self-attributed failure."
        assert not violations(ok) and violations(bad)
        print("selftest ok")
        return 0
    v = violations(open(sys.argv[1]).read())
    for s in v[:20]:
        print("UNSCOPED:", s[:120])
    print(f"{len(v)} unscoped result sentence(s)")
    return 1 if v else 0

if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())
EOF

Corpus question first, then registration, then the papers.

## Which corpus — split by what each test needs

The six filed predictions (P-r1…P-q1) are backtests: they need ground truth — known catches, time-sliced states, a sealed history. Only latent_welfare has that. They cannot run on MATS papers at all. The MATS corpus serves the two tests latent_welfare cannot host: the forward test (form a research question from cold material — latent_welfare already has its question) and the generalization test (do ELICIT's five mismatch categories work outside the project that generated them).

**Steelman for latent_welfare:** it is the only corpus where we can tell a good elicited question from a plausible dud — the record says which questions mattered, when they became askable, and what fell when pressed. It's contamination-proof (private, post-cutoff). Its infrastructure exists (slices, blind keys, provenance). Its stakes are real: queue item 1 alone could change a submitted paper's claim. And the complexity you're worried about is the ecology the harness targets — a clean corpus would test an easier problem than the one we actually have. The confound worry also inverts: on latent_welfare we spent a retro mapping the confounds, so we can see them; on MATS the confounds are unknown and the biggest one — memory posing as insight — is invisible from inside the output.

**What MATS buys:** external validity (different authors, no shared vocabulary with our tooling); the right artifact type (finished justification-genre papers — what the tool would meet in the wild, not provenance records); the forward test; and cheapness (one self-contained PDF, no slicing, no history reconstruction). **A good MATS example** is post-cutoff or obscure (less memory), carries quantitative claims with stated numbers (so claim-beside-number pairing works inside one document), states its predictions or hypotheses somewhere, and has public code so an elicited question can ground itself by re-derivation.

## Registered predictions — filing to disk before opening any PDF

content.content:
R1D1 - Is Reasoning in Language Models
           Mediated by a Single Direction?

           Executive Summary
Sample generations showing intervention effects:




           What problem am I trying to solve?

           I investigated whether a "reasoning direction" exists in the activation space of large language
           models, inspired by the recent paper "Refusal in Large Language Models as Mediated by a
           Single Direction" by Arditi et al. While the original paper compared activations from the same
           model on both harmless and harmful prompts, I explored a different approach by comparing
           activations between reasoning and non-reasoning models on identical prompts. I
           hypothesized that by subtracting the non-reasoning model's activations from the reasoning
           model's activations, I could identify a direction in activation space that could influence
           reasoning capabilities.

           This investigation was motivated by the growing importance of reasoning abilities in LLMs,
           where models that explicitly reason through problems step-by-step often achieve higher
           accuracy than those that generate answers directly. Understanding the mechanistic basis of
           reasoning could help enhance reasoning capabilities in smaller models or identify
           components critical for alignment.

           High-level takeaways

               1.​ Direction Identification: I calculated potential reasoning directions by comparing
                   activations from a non-reasoning model (Llama-3 8B) and a reasoning model
        (DeepSeek R1 Distill Llama3-8B) on identical GSM8K math problems.​

   2.​ Initial Approach Failed: My original hypothesis was that adding the calculated
       reasoning direction to the non-reasoning model would induce reasoning behavior.
       However, these interventions produced negligible effects regardless of strength or
       layer. The non-reasoning model continued to generate direct answers without
       showing any signs of explicit reasoning. This failure led me to try the inverse
       approach - applying the direction to the reasoning model instead.​

   3.​ Successful Bidirectional Control: When applying the difference direction to the
       reasoning model, I discovered it could either enhance or suppress reasoning
       behavior depending on the strength and layer of application.​

   4.​ Layer Specificity: Early layers (1-3) showed the strongest effects on reasoning
       behavior, while later layers (19+) showed minimal impact. This pattern suggests that
       reasoning behavior may be established early in the network's processing.​

   5.​ Control Experiments: I conducted additional experiments using pure original
       activations or pure reasoning activations (instead of their difference). These
       interventions also changed the model's behavior - both could induce similar ‘anxiety’
       within the reasoning process - but neither immediately demonstrated the bidirectional
       control (ability to both enhance and eliminate reasoning) observed with the difference
       direction.​



Key Experiments

As shown in the first graph above, applying the reasoning direction at different layers affects
the model's token production in varying ways. The y-axis shows the difference in average
token count for 5 simple math problems between intervened and baseline generations, while
the x-axis shows the layer where the intervention was applied. The pronounced effects in
early layers (0-3) and diminishing impact in later layers provide valuable insights into where
reasoning may be processed in the model.

For a deeper analysis, I measured tokens inside thinking tags (<think>...</think>)
separately from tokens outside these tags, as shown in the second graph. This revealed that
interventions primarily affected the tokens inside thinking sections while leaving the final
answer (outside thinking) relatively unchanged. This supports the hypothesis that the
identified direction is specifically modulating reasoning behavior rather than changing the
model's knowledge.

The example generations demonstrate the range of effects observed. When adding the
direction to layer 1 with strength 0.1, the model became significantly more verbose and
hesitant in its reasoning. Conversely, when adding the direction to layer 0 with strength -0.1,
reasoning was sometimes eliminated completely, seemingly turning the reasoning model into
its non-reasoning ‘predecessor’.

These experiments reveal that we can systematically influence reasoning behavior through
targeted interventions in activation space. While more research would be needed to fully
characterize a "reasoning direction," these findings provide evidence that reasoning
capabilities in R1-like large language models have identifiable features that can be
manipulated to control reasoning behavior.
 Detailed Analysis
Background and Related Work

This work is inspired by the paper "Refusal in Large Language Models as Mediated by a
Single Direction" by Arditi et al., which demonstrated that refusal behavior in LLMs can be
controlled by manipulating a single direction in activation space. Their methodology involved
capturing the difference in activations between a model responding to harmful versus
harmless prompts, and showed this direction could be used to suppress refusal behavior.

Recently, a new class of LLMs known as "reasoning models" has emerged. Models like
DeepSeek's R1 models are trained to explicitly reason through problems before providing
answers, using structures like <think>...</think> tags. This reasoning approach has
been shown to improve performance across various benchmarks, especially on
mathematical and logical reasoning tasks.

Unlike refusal behavior, reasoning cannot be easily induced through prompting alone.
Standard models like Llama-3 can be prompted to "think step by step," but reasoning models
perform this behavior more consistently and effectively because they've been specifically
fine-tuned for this capability.

Detailed Methodology

Models and Setup

   ●​ Non-reasoning model: Llama-3 8B Instruct
   ●​ Reasoning model: DeepSeek R1 Distill Llama-8B
   ●​ Both models were loaded using HookedTransformer from TransformerLens for
      activation access

Data and Prompt Processing

   ●​   Primary dataset: GSM8K mathematical reasoning problems
   ●​   Secondary dataset: 10 simple toy math problems (e.g., "What is 2+2?")
   ●​   All prompts were processed using the models' respective chat templates
   ●​   For each model, activations were collected from the residual stream at pre-attention,
        mid-attention, and post-attention points

Direction Calculation

For each layer and activation point (pre/mid/post), I calculated:

   1.​ The mean activation across a batch of examples
   2.​ The difference between reasoning and non-reasoning activations
   3.​ Normalized this difference to create a unit vector representing the "reasoning
       direction"

Intervention Method

To test these directions, I implemented a hook function that adds the direction vector to the
model's activations during generation:

def reasoning_enhancement_hook(
      activation: Tensor,
     hook: HookPoint,
     direction: Tensor,
     strength: float = 1.0
):
     return activation + (strength * direction.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0))


I then experimented with these hooks across different:

      ●​   Layers (0-30)
      ●​   Strength values (-0.1, -0.05, 0.05, 0.1)
      ●​   Direction types (difference, original, reasoning)
      ●​   Models (non-reasoning, reasoning)
      ●​   Activation points (pre/mid/post)

Experimental Results

Non-Reasoning Model Interventions

Initial attempts to induce reasoning behavior in the non-reasoning model by adding the
reasoning direction were unsuccessful. The model maintained its typical response pattern
regardless of intervention strength or layer. This suggests that:

      1.​ The reasoning capability may require more than a single direction modification
      2.​ The base model may lack necessary structures to support explicit reasoning behavior

Reasoning Model Interventions

When applying these same directions to the reasoning model, I observed significant effects:

Enhanced Reasoning: With certain strength values in most layers, the model produced:

      ●​   Increased token count (sometimes by 100+ tokens)
      ●​   More hesitant, uncertain reasoning
      ●​   Multiple reconsiderations and backtracking
      ●​   Exploration of alternative interpretations of even simple problems
      ●​   Interestingly, if you push the strength to 0.1-0.2 the output simply becomes
           <think>:




Suppressed Reasoning: With other strength values in specific layers (particularly layer 0),
the model sometimes:

      ●​ Eliminated reasoning tokens completely
      ●​ Skipped the <think> section entirely
      ●​ Provided only the direct answer
 Layer Specificity: The most pronounced effects were observed in early layers (0-3), with
effects generally diminishing in later layers (19+). This suggests reasoning behavior may be
established early in the network's processing pipeline.

Control Experiments

To validate that the difference direction was capturing something specific about reasoning, I
conducted control experiments:

   1.​ Randomly generated activations: Adding randomly generated actications.
   2.​ Original activations only: Adding just the non-reasoning model's activations
   3.​ Reasoning activations only: Adding just the reasoning model's activations



As expected when applying randomly generated (around the mean of actual generations)
activations, the model appeared to produce random tokens.

Both controls altered the model's output length and style, but neither produced the
bidirectional control (both enhancing and suppressing reasoning) observed with the
difference direction. However, given the time and compute constraints this warrants further
investigation.




Limitations and Future Work

This investigation has several limitations:

   1.​ Compute constraints: Limited testing to specific directions, layers and strength
       values
   2.​ Model specificity: Results may not generalize to other model architectures or sizes
   3.​ Task limitation: Only tested on mathematical reasoning tasks
   4.​ Intervention simplicity: Only tested additive interventions, not more complex
       transformations
   5.​ Reasoning quality assessment: This study equated token count with reasoning but
       didn't assess whether improved reasoning led to better accuracy or problem-solving.
